title: Matryoshka Agent: Unfolding Sub-Agents for Long-Horizon Machine Learning Engineering

images.desc:
1 Introduction


Large Language Models (LLMs) have developed from static question-answering (QA) chatbots to autonomous agents that are capable of solving complex, multi-step challenges through interaction with real-world environments chan2024mle ; jimenez2023swe ; qiang2025mledojo ; zhou2023webarena ; merrill2026terminal ; wei2025browsecomp ; yao2024tau ; xie2024osworld ; patwardhan2025gdpval .
Within this expanding landscape, a new class of performance-optimization agentic tasks has emerged, where the goal is not merely to complete a single executable objective, but to progressively improve solution quality through feedback from the environment ouyang2025kernelbench ; press2025algotune ; rank2026posttrainbench . These tasks are typically characterized by several fundamental challenges.
First, long-horizon interaction naturally produces growing contexts, with execution logs, intermediate outputs, and debugging feedback accumulated across rounds du2025deepresearch ; wei2025browsecomp .
Second, these tasks involve large, open-ended action and observation spaces, where diverse observations can induce a broad range of subsequent refinement choices phan2025humanity ; merrill2026terminal ; ouyang2025kernelbench ; press2025algotune .
Third, environment interactions often incur substantial wall-clock and computational cost, making both inference-time exploration and training-time data collection expensive starace2025paperbench ; huang2023mlagentbench ; rank2026posttrainbench .
Machine Learning Engineering (MLE) tasks, characterized by their dependency on task-specific datasets with diverse modalities (e.g., images, text), schemas, data distributions, and evaluation objectives, constitute a particularly challenging and representative instantiation of these difficulties nam2025mle ; jing2024dsbench ; chan2024mle ; qiang2025mlesmith ; huang2023mlagentbench .
Consequently, effective MLE agents must combine strong coding and debugging skills with deep domain understanding and the ability to systematically explore and exploit diverse methodological alternatives jiang2025aide ; li2024autokaggle ; yang2025r ; guo2024ds ; nam2025mle ; toledo2025ai , which inevitably requires accumulating extensive history contexts that include redundant information.
Furthermore, the practical execution of MLE code is often computationally intensive and time-consuming, especially for large-scale datasets. The need to handle long contexts under noisy and partially redundant histories, the substantial time and computational costs of environment interaction, and the requirement for sustained exploration and iterative refinement jointly pose significant challenges for agents to effectively solve this important yet highly complex class of tasks.


In response to these challenges, we propose Matryoshka Agent, a hierarchical framework for long-horizon
MLE tasks. Matryoshka Agent separates iterative performance optimization into three coordinated layers. Orchestrator serves as the high-level decision layer: it maintains a compact cross-round state over previous instructions, summarized outcomes, and evaluation scores, and decides which
solution direction to refine next.
Sub-Agents serve as the execution layer: they are instantiated with fresh contexts to implement, run, and debug concrete solution attempts through direct environment interaction.
Tools mediate between these layers by formatting Orchestrator instructions, injecting selected references from previous attempts, launching Sub-Agents, and returning structured summaries and
scores. This design creates an efficient separation between strategic evolution and concrete execution, reducing long-context burden while preserving key information for iterative refinement.
Beyond the inference-time framework, Matryoshka Agent further develop a training paradigm tailored to expensive performance-optimization tasks.
During training, Solution Refinement Tree–based sampling reuses shared execution prefixes and collects structured comparisons among alternative refinements from common states.
These comparisons provide trajectory-level preference signals for optimizing the Orchestrator with online ranking-based reinforcement learning, while successful execution trajectories being
used to improve Sub-Agents.


Figure 1: Overview of Matryoshka Agent. Upper: Interaction Logic among the three-layered structure. Lower: Training Paradigm with Solution Refinement Tree–based sampling.


Our contributions can be summarized as follows:


• 

We propose Matryoshka Agent, a hierarchical MLE agent framework that decouples high-level
orchestration from low-level code execution through structured tool-
mediated feedback.



• 

We introduce a training paradigm based on Solution Refinement Tree–based sampling and
trajectory-level ranking optimization, enabling efficient Orchestrator learning from costly
environment interactions while supporting Sub-Agent improvement from successful executions.



• 

We evaluate and analyze Matryoshka Agent extensively across a wide range of MLE tasks with diverse model types, scales, and combinations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both Matryoshka Agent and the training paradigm.

4.5 Cumulated Context Length


Figure 2: Cumulated Context Length across rounds. X-axis denotes the number of rounds, while y-axis denotes the token count in units of 10310^{3}. Shaded areas indicate the standard deviation. Contexts of Dojo Agent and Orchestrator are averaged over tasks, while contexts of Sub-Agents are averaged per round over tasks.


A core advantage of Matryoshka Agent lies in its effective and clean separation of context management between the Orchestrator and the Sub-Agents. As interaction rounds with the environment increase, each sub-agent maintains an independent context with a fixed upper bound that does not grow with the number of interactions. At the same time, although the Orchestrator’s context does grow over time, its growth rate remains modest even as the interaction horizon becomes long. As a result, Matryoshka Agent remains robust even under extreme settings with very long time periods and a large number of interactions, whereas the context of the Dojo Agent expands more rapidly. Figure 2 illustrates the evolution of context length for the Orchestrator, the Sub-Agents, and the Dojo Agent as the number of interaction rounds increases. The figure shows that the Orchestrator’s context length grows at a slower rate than that of the Dojo Agent, while the Sub-Agents’ context lengths remain stable across interaction rounds due to their independence. We further discuss context length scaling in Appendix F
